subtype: Approach: falling for easy-money schemes online [Pitfall]
passage: I'm Gurleen, and for twenty minutes I was sure I was a genius. Minakshi showed me an ad in a game: send 1,500 rupees, get 3,000 back in a week, no risk. I had exactly that saved from two years of allowance. I was already spending the extra 1,500 in my head, a new bag, treats for my cousins. My thumb was over the send button when Mummy walked in and asked why I looked so pale. I showed her the phone. She didn't shout. She said offers that double your money in days are almost always frauds, and that if the money were real, nobody would need to advertise it in a game. We closed it, and she showed me how to report the ad. I felt silly, then relieved.

qa.q: How much did the ad ask Gurleen to send?
qa.a: The ad asked Gurleen to send 1,500 rupees.

qa.q: What was Gurleen feeling while imagining the extra money, and afterwards?
qa.a: Gurleen felt excited and sure of being a genius, and afterwards felt silly and then relieved.

qa.q: What could Gurleen do the next time an offer promises fast money?
qa.a: Gurleen could show it to a parent or another adult first, since a promise of doubled money in days is a warning sign.

qa.q: How might Mummy have felt when she saw the phone?
qa.a: Mummy was probably worried and protective, yet stayed calm, since she didn't shout but explained and helped report the ad.

grounding: A teen imagines quick success from an online promise to double savings and nearly sends money before a parent explains it is likely a fraud.

subtype: Approach: falling for easy-money schemes online [Pitfall]
passage:
Parent's note, Thursday night
This evening Vijay came to me with his phone and his savings tin. A video had promised that money put into a “game app” today would double in a week, “guaranteed”. It showed a boy his age holding up a new phone. Vijay had already typed his savings amount into the app's payment page and wanted my card to finish it.
He was excited in a way I recognised: he had already spent the doubled money in his head. His friend Sarika had forwarded the same link and was about to pay too.
I asked him to sit with me before pressing anything. We looked up the app's name together and found many complaints. I explained that anything promising to double money quickly is almost always a fraud, and that real saving is slow. He was quiet, then disappointed, then relieved.
We deleted the app. He messaged Sarika at once: “Don't pay. It's a scam. Ask your mum."

qa.a: That money put into a game app today would double in a week, guaranteed.

qa.q: How did Vijay feel as the conversation went on?
qa.a: Vijay was excited at first, then quiet and disappointed, and finally relieved.

qa.q: What could Vijay do the next time such an offer appears?
qa.a: Pause and show a parent before paying, and look up complaints, since quick-doubling promises are usually frauds.

qa.q: How might Sarika feel getting Vijay's message?
qa.a: Sarika may feel startled and a bit embarrassed, but relieved to be warned before paying.

grounding: A parent notes a teen nearly sending savings to a double-your-money game app before the parent explains that such offers are usually frauds.

subtype: Approach: falling for easy-money schemes online [Pitfall]
passage:
Sunday
Nearly did something really dumb today.
Divyansh showed me an ad inside a game: “Invest your pocket money, get double in 7 days. 100% safe.” There were screenshots of people's payments, all green ticks. I have 1,800 saved for a football. Double would be 3,600. I started picturing the boots too.
I went to Baba to ask for help paying on his phone, trying to make it sound small. He read the ad for about ten seconds and put the phone face down.
He said, “Arnab, if a stranger could double money in seven days, why would they need your 1,800?” Then he showed me a news report about the same kind of app, where children lost everything they put in.
I felt stupid, then angry at the ad, then just glad. I texted Divyansh not to do it either.
The football still costs what it costs. Six more weeks.

qa.q: How much had Arnab saved for the football?
How did Arnab feel after Baba's question?
qa.a: Arnab felt stupid, then angry at the ad, and finally glad not to have paid.

qa.q: What check could Arnab use on the next offer like this?
qa.a: Ask Baba's question, why would a stranger need my money if they can double it, and show a parent before paying.

qa.q: What might Divyansh feel getting Arnab's text?
qa.a: Divyansh may feel caught out but relieved, since the warning came before any money was sent.

grounding: Shows a teen nearly sending savings to an online double-in-a-week offer before a parent explains that such offers are usually frauds.
